activity.title: Fear Itself and Four Freedoms

readings.attribution: Franklin D. Roosevelt, inaugural address, March 4, 1933. Public domain (U.S. government work).
readings.body:
"So, first of all, let me assert my firm belief that the only thing we have to fear is fear itself—nameless, unreasoning, unjustified terror which paralyzes needed efforts to convert retreat into advance."

"This Nation asks for action, and action now."

"Our greatest primary task is to put people to work."

Context: When Roosevelt spoke, about one worker in four was unemployed, and banks in many states had closed their doors to stop panicked depositors from withdrawing their money.
readings.title: Franklin D. Roosevelt, First Inaugural Address (1933), excerpts

readings.attribution: Franklin D. Roosevelt, annual message to Congress, January 6, 1941. Public domain (U.S. government work).
readings.body:
"In the future days, which we seek to make secure, we look forward to a world founded upon four essential human freedoms.
The first is freedom of speech and expression—everywhere in the world.
The second is freedom of every person to worship God in his own way—everywhere in the world.
The third is freedom from want—which, translated into world terms, means economic understandings which will secure to every nation a healthy peacetime life for its inhabitants—everywhere in the world.
The fourth is freedom from fear—which, translated into world terms, means a world-wide reduction of armaments to such a point and in such a thorough fashion that no nation will be in a position to commit an act of physical aggression against any neighbor—anywhere in the world."

Context: Roosevelt spoke eleven months before the attack on Pearl Harbor, when the United States was not yet at war but Britain was fighting Germany almost alone.
